title: Why ‘meet me at the station’ needs one more number in Seoul
photoAlt: Pedestrians on a Myeongdong shopping street beneath closely packed shop signs
photoContext: Myeongdong street scene, photographed by Harry Angara. Unsplash License: https://unsplash.com/license . Source: https://unsplash.com/photos/HAI-xwFpFg4 . Context photograph, not the station exit or imagined bakery in this story.
excerpt: You and your friend have reached the same station. So why can’t you find each other? A small Seoul meeting habit, three useful Korean lines and a better way to start your walk.
question: What is the easiest meeting point to explain to a newcomer in your city?

expressions.translation: Which exit are we meeting at?

expressions.meaning: See you at the bakery in front of the station.
expressions.translation: See you tomorrow at the bakery in front of the station.

body:
Imagine this: you have arrived at a Seoul subway station, right on time. Your friend sends a message saying she has arrived too. You scan the pavement, lift your phone and turn around. No friend. She sends a photograph of a bakery. You send a photograph of a bus stop. Both pictures have the same station name in them. Somehow, you have managed to be in the same place and nowhere near each other.

The missing detail might be a single number. In Seoul, a plan to meet at a station often comes with an exit number attached. That number can be the difference between spotting a familiar face immediately and spending your first conversation describing whatever shop happens to be behind you.

## The station has several front doors

Think of a station as a building with several front doors opening onto different streets. The train gets you to the building; choosing an exit gets you to the right doorstep. Seoul’s official tourism guide explains that subway exits are numbered and station signs use Korean and English. Once you start looking for those numbers, the station becomes easier to read. You are choosing a particular way up to the street.

That is why ‘I’m at the station’ can leave so much unsaid. Are you still on the platform? Beside a ticket gate? Already outdoors? An exit number narrows the search, but one more detail helps: above ground or below? The Institute for Basic Science’s guide for international residents describes station exits as common meeting points, with street level the usual assumption unless people agree otherwise.

Keep the line number and exit number separate. Line 2 tells you which train service you are using; Exit 2 tells you which opening you are looking for at a particular station. Write the station name alongside the exit when sharing a plan. Just sending “Exit 2” is rather like sending someone a house number without the street.

## A small habit of making plans

This is a useful bit of everyday Korean life to notice. A friend can send a station name, an exit and a time without writing a full address. For someone familiar with that station, the message may feel perfectly complete. A newcomer may need a photograph or a map pin as well. Asking for one is sensible, especially when the person giving directions has walked that route for years.

If your friend writes 3번 출구, you can recognise the number before you can read the whole phrase. 번 (beon) marks the numbered item. Try spotting that short combination on a sign, then compare it with the message on your phone. It is a satisfying little reading exercise with an immediate answer.

The habit also gives an outing a gentle beginning. You can meet before deciding which restaurant to try, rather than making one person search the lanes alone. Picture two friends comparing dinner ideas beside an exit sign. One has saved a noodle shop; the other has noticed a bakery. Before either person has ordered anything, they already have something to talk about.

## Three lines before you climb the stairs

Here is a short practice conversation. For this example, imagine a bakery beside your agreed exit. It is an invented meeting place, not a recommendation for a real shop. You have reached the station and want to check where to go next.

You: 몇 번 출구예요? (myeot beon chulguyeyo?) ‘Which exit is it?’

Friend: 3번 출구 밖에서 만나요. (sam beon chulgu bakkeseo mannayo.) ‘Let’s meet outside Exit 3.’

You: 역 앞 빵집에서 봬요. (yeok ap ppangjibeseo bwaeyo.) ‘See you at the bakery in front of the station.’

Listen for 출구 (chulgu), meaning exit, and 밖 (bak), meaning outside. The number 3 here is 삼 (sam), so 3번 is sam beon. You may have learned 셋 (set) when counting three things. Exit numbers use the other Korean number set, the same one used for numbered labels. You can practise the whole bakery sentence in Sori’s existing lesson rather than trying to remember every word separately.

## The last part of the journey

Before leaving the station, take a moment to look at the neighborhood map. Find your destination and the exit nearest to it, then follow the signs. An exit number identifies an opening, not your whole walking route. When you reach the pavement, check which way the shop or meeting point lies. Turning around once to compare the street with your map is much easier than confidently walking several blocks in the wrong direction.

There is a similar distinction when you need an elevator. The exit closest to your destination may not be the entrance that suits your journey. Seoul’s city website lists station accessibility facilities, including elevators and escalators. Check the station’s current signs or ask staff about the route from platform to street, particularly with a suitcase, stroller or wheelchair. A facility count alone does not tell you exactly where to emerge.

If the meeting needs to move to another entrance, send the new location before either person sets off. A clear photograph of the sign and a message saying whether you are upstairs or downstairs can resolve a surprising amount. Stand somewhere that leaves the entrance clear while you wait. There is no advantage to being easy to spot if everyone else has to squeeze around you.

## Give the meeting point a name

Back at our imaginary bakery, your friend finally appears. Now 빵집 (ppangjip), bakery, means something you can see through a window. Perhaps you point at 소보로빵 (soboroppang), the bun with a crumbly topping, and ask whether to buy one for the walk. The location that caused all that confusion has become the first small stop of the afternoon.

That is the pleasant part of learning these practical phrases. A sentence about directions can become a sentence about seeing someone. Keep the station name, check the exit number and agree on which side of the stairs you mean. Then put the phone away when your friend arrives. What is the meeting point in your own city that everyone understands, until someone visits for the first time?

title: Why is there a basket of lettuce at Korean barbecue?
photoAlt: Grilled pork belly served Korean barbecue style
photoContext: Samgyeopsal, grilled pork belly. Photograph by jinsoo jang, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.
excerpt: One leaf, a little rice and a piece of pork. Learn how to make a ssam, offer one to someone else and negotiate the last bite in Korean.
question: What would you put in a wrap for someone you know well?

sources.label: National Folk Museum of Korea, Ssam (leaf wraps)
Korea Tourism Organization, Leaf Wraps and Rice
Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, Korea’s food-wrapping tradition

expressions.meaning: How do you wrap this to eat it?
expressions.translation: How do you make a wrap with a perilla leaf?

expressions.meaning: Shall I make you a wrap?
expressions.translation: Shall I make yours without garlic?

expressions.meaning: Would you like the last piece?
expressions.translation: Would you like a piece of this meat?
Could we have more rice here, please?

body:
Someone puts a basket of lettuce beside the grill. You reach for a leaf, then pause. There is no salad bowl. Across the table, your friend has a leaf open on her palm. She adds a piece of pork, barely a spoonful of rice and a dab of reddish paste. She folds the edges in and eats the whole thing. By the time you have decided what to put in yours, she is already making another.

Welcome to Korea 101. Today we’re pulling up a chair at a Korean barbecue table. We’ll make one very small dinner decision together: what goes into a single leaf? Along the way, you’ll learn how to ask a friend to show you, how to offer someone a bite, and what to say when the last piece of pork is still sitting on the grill.

## One leaf, one bite

The little parcel is a 쌈 (ssam). The verb 싸다 (ssada) means “to wrap.” You can hear the same verb when someone talks about wrapping a present. At dinner, though, the object might be a slippery piece of grilled pork belly. If you are making your first ssam, try a leaf about the size of your palm. Put the meat in the middle, fold the bottom edge up and bring the sides together. If the first one falls apart, eat what you have and try a smaller filling on the next round.

Now try two with exactly the same pork. Make the first with lettuce, 상추 (sangchu). For the second, pick a 깻잎 (kkaennip), a perilla leaf. The lettuce gives a cool crunch and then gets out of the way. The perilla has a scent that stays with you after the meat is gone. You may understand why the person beside you has been carefully peeling those leaves apart all evening. Or you may go straight back to the lettuce. Either way, you’ve learned something about your own order.

## How the grill got into the picture

If your introduction to ssam was a barbecue restaurant, it is easy to imagine that grilled meat came first and someone invented a leafy wrapper to go with it. A cookbook published in 1924 offers a different picture. As the National Folk Museum of Korea notes, it described napa cabbage as a common wrapper. You could bring leaves and cooked rice to a table and already have the beginnings of a meal.

That older idea is still right there on a restaurant sign. Look for 쌈밥 (ssambap). You already know 쌈, and 밥 is cooked rice. At a ssambap restaurant, the selection of leaves can be worth paying attention to in its own right. One might be crisp and raw, another cabbage leaf tender enough to fold over with a fingertip. The Korea Tourism Organization describes versions with fish as well as meat. A piece of fish tucked into soft cabbage makes a very different lunch from pork hot off the grill.

## The brown pot between the chopsticks

Back at our barbecue table, the reddish-brown paste is 쌈장 (ssamjang). It is usually made with 된장 (doenjang, fermented soybean paste) and 고추장 (gochujang, red pepper paste). Recipes vary. Start with a little on the tip of a chopstick. That leaves room to taste the pork, and you can always add more to the next bite. Garlic, sliced chillies or kimchi might be within reach too. You can leave every one of them on its plate.

There is a practical reason to start small. Once your friend has folded a generous leaf around two pieces of pork, rice and a whole garlic clove, that is exactly when someone will ask her a question. Give her a moment. A nod and a laugh are usually all she can manage. When it is your turn to talk, try 이거 어떻게 싸 먹어요? (igeo eotteoke ssa meogeoyo?), “How do you wrap this to eat it?” Someone can answer that question with their hands even if you don’t catch every word.

## When someone makes one for you

Suppose your friend sets a finished wrap on your plate. She remembered you skipped the raw garlic last time. Without saying much, she has made something that is yours down to the last ingredient. If you’d like to return the gesture, ask 쌈 하나 싸 드릴까요? (ssam hana ssa deurilkkayo?), “Shall I make you a wrap?” The ending 드릴까요 makes the offer polite. You can use the same ending when offering to pour someone water. Pause for the answer, especially if you’ve only just met.

Later, there is one piece of pork left. Everyone can see it. If you want to offer it around, 마지막 한 점 드실래요? (majimak han jeom deusillaeyo?) means “Would you like the last piece?” Listen for 점 (jeom). It is a handy word for a piece of meat or fish. A friend might say 반씩 먹어요 (banssik meogeoyo), “Let’s have half each.” If someone offers it to you and you want it, 네, 잘 먹을게요 (ne, jal meogeulgeyo), “Yes, thank you, I’ll enjoy it,” gives them an answer and lets dinner carry on.

## Something to try at your next meal

You can practise this at home with one lettuce leaf and a little leftover rice. Say 쌈 as you pick up the leaf. Ask someone whether they’d like one before you start choosing their filling. Then let them make one for you. Even people eating from exactly the same dishes rarely end up with the same bite.

If someone at your table offered to make you a ssam tonight, what would you ask them to put inside? And is there anything you would quietly ask them to leave out?
